ocar.opportunity: Proofreading split and merge errors is the rate-limiting step in synapse-resolution connectomics, so a shared multi-species training set could let one vision model serve mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly volumes.
ocar.challenge: Proofreading labels are fragmented by species and error type, and it is unclear whether a single model can reach human-level accuracy, stay calibrated, and adapt cheaply when the next brain looks different.
ocar.action: Brown, Farkas, Razgar, and Boyden (arXiv, 2026) release ConnectomeBench2, with over 716,485 expert-labeled proofreading decisions and more than 4,500,000 associated images spanning four open connectomes, then train a Vision Transformer with shared encoders for mesh geometry and electron microscopy on split correction, merge identification, and merge-correction mask generation.
ocar.resolution: A single ViT reaches human-level accuracy across species for split error correction and merge error identification, with performance scaling with data size and modality. The model is well-calibrated in distribution; distribution-distance measures predict degradation on unseen data; connectomics-specific pretraining outperforms ImageNet for new species; and at a budget of K = 300 operations on leave-one-species-out mouse, facility-location and batch-Fisher selection beat random sampling on merge identification, though absolute performance at that budget remains well below deployment.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag lossy 2D slice rendering versus full 3D EM cutouts, Vision-Transformer-only architectural coverage, and species imbalance, and they present the benchmark as infrastructure for 3D embeddings, other architectures, and cheaper adaptation to new regions.

summaries.beginner: Fixing computer mistakes in 3D brain maps still takes huge amounts of human time. This team released a shared test set from mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly brains and showed that one vision model can match people on many of those fixes.
summaries.intermediate: Brown, Farkas, Razgar, and Boyden (arXiv, 2026) introduce ConnectomeBench2, a unified proofreading benchmark with over 716,485 expert decisions and more than 4.5 million images from four open connectomes. A Vision Transformer with shared mesh and EM encoders is trained on split correction, merge identification, and merge-correction masks. Joint training matches or exceeds species-specific models; in-distribution calibration is strong; Mahalanobis distance provides a label-free shift signal; and connectomics pretraining plus active learning reduce the labels needed to touch a new species. Data and code are released on Hugging Face and GitHub.
summaries.advanced: Human-level claims are for split correction and merge identification, not a blanket claim that merge-mask generation matches experts. Active-learning gains at K = 300 on held-out mouse still leave performance far below a deployable proofreader for a new species. 2D slice renders are lossy relative to 3D cutouts; evaluations emphasize ViTs rather than 3D CNNs or point-cloud models; and sample counts are unbalanced across species, which the authors say should temper leave-one-species-out claims.

plain_language_summary: Fixing computer mistakes in 3D brain maps still takes huge amounts of human time. This team released a shared test set from mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly brains and showed that one vision model can match people on many of those fixes.

ocar.opportunity: Electron-microscopy volumes collected for fly connectomics already contain mitochondria, so the same images can be mined for subcellular metabolism without a new acquisition.
ocar.challenge: How mitochondrial size, placement, and appearance vary by cell type, synapse polarity, and brain region at whole-central-brain scale has not been measured.
ocar.action: Longden, Rivlin, Januszewski, Neace, Scheffer, Berg and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2026) extract, classify, and measure approximately 6 million mitochondria from the Drosophila Hemibrain, annotate location, orientation, voxel size, and appearance (dark/dense, light/sparse, or medium), link each synapse to its closest mitochondrion, and add the objects to neuPrint.
ocar.resolution: Mitochondria are larger and closer at presynapses than postsynapses, and presynapses typically have a mitochondrion within one micron, but Kenyon cells have unusually small, sparse mitochondria near only about half of presynapses. Inhibitory neurons devote a greater fraction of cell volume to mitochondria than excitatory cells; dopaminergic and glutamatergic neurons show distinctive positioning or light appearance; and synapses with more postsynaptic partners have larger presynaptic mitochondria and more distant postsynaptic mitochondria.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the neuPrint release as a public substrate for further cell-type and regional analyses rather than a finished physiological account of why these patterns exist.

summaries.beginner: Connectome pictures of the fly brain also show mitochondria, the cell’s energy factories. This team catalogued millions of them, found that different neuron types place and size them differently, and put the catalog online so others can search it.
summaries.intermediate: Longden et al. (bioRxiv, 2026; Janelia FlyEM and collaborators) mine the Drosophila Hemibrain for approximately 6 million mitochondria, most of them among more than 20 thousand neurons and over 5500 cell types. Each organelle is labeled for location, orientation, size, and appearance, and each synapse is linked to its nearest mitochondrion. Presynaptic mitochondria are typically larger and closer (within one micron) than postsynaptic ones, while Kenyon cells are an exception with small, sparse mitochondria near only about half of presynapses. Inhibitory, dopaminergic, and glutamatergic classes show further differences in occupancy, placement, or appearance. The objects are queryable in neuPrint as neuronal subcellular components.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint reuse of Hemibrain EM, not a new volume or live imaging of mitochondrial dynamics. Appearance classes (dark/dense, light/sparse, medium) are morphological, not direct metabolic assays. Kenyon-cell and transmitter-class claims are correlative with Hemibrain cell types; causal links to learning, memory, or synapse strength are not tested here. Coverage is the central brain Hemibrain, not a complete adult CNS.

plain_language_summary: Connectome pictures of the fly brain also show mitochondria, the cell’s energy factories. This team catalogued millions of them, found that different neuron types place and size them differently, and put the catalog online so others can search it.

ocar.opportunity: Flies must judge attraction versus aversion in messy natural scenes, not only in simple lab odors, so a brain-wide wiring map could show where innate and learned valences meet.
ocar.challenge: Prior valence work in Drosophila has focused on the lateral horn (LH) and mushroom body (MB) with synthetic stimuli, leaving the circuit for natural multimodal objects unclear.
ocar.action: Wang, Yang, Liu, Sun and colleagues (Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 2026) use brain-wide connectome analysis to place the superior protocerebrum (SP) as a convergence–divergence bottleneck that collects LH and MB inputs and broadcasts especially to the central complex.
ocar.resolution: They argue that SP resembles an autoencoder bottleneck: LH neurons pool ethologically related innate valences (unimodal food odors, or multimodal wind and temperature as ‘lousy weather’), opponent attraction and aversion are combined in SP, and MB learned valences update innate LH signals. Attractive versus aversive inputs arrive via excitatory versus inhibitory synapses onto single SP neurons with opposite dendritic organizations.
ocar.future_work: The paper highlights SP as a candidate general motif for complex valence; physiological tests of the autoencoder analogy and of dendritic opponent integration are left open.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies must decide what is good or bad in a messy world, not just in a simple lab smell. This study uses a whole-brain wiring map to argue that a region called the superior protocerebrum mixes inborn and learned likes and dislikes before sending a compact signal onward.
summaries.intermediate: Wang et al. (Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 2026) analyze Drosophila connectomes to argue that the evolutionarily conserved superior protocerebrum (SP) integrates brain-wide multimodal inputs mainly via the lateral horn and mushroom body and sends widespread outputs, especially to the central complex. They describe a convergence–divergence layout resembling an autoencoder, with SP as the bottleneck for low-dimensional valence. LH inputs can be unimodal (diverse food odors) or multimodal (wind and temperature as poor weather); MB learned valences update innate LH signals; and single SP neurons combine attraction and aversion through excitatory versus inhibitory synapses with opposite dendritic organization. The work is a circuit-anatomy study of valence integration, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: The autoencoder analogy is an architectural reading of connectivity, not a trained model or a demonstration that SP activity is low-dimensional. Claims about ‘robust valence detection in natural environments’ are inferred from wiring and known LH/MB roles rather than new freely behaving physiology in this paper. Opponent dendritic organization is anatomical; whether it computes a signed valence sum in vivo is untested here.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies must decide what is good or bad in a messy world, not just in a simple lab smell. This study uses a whole-brain wiring map to argue that a region called the superior protocerebrum mixes inborn and learned likes and dislikes before sending a compact signal onward.

ocar.opportunity: Large-volume serial electron microscopy needs reliable libraries of ultrathin sections, but existing tape- and magnet-based collectors (ATUM, MagC, GAUSS-EM) often demand specialized hardware or infrastructure.
ocar.challenge: Cost, hardware, and setup still limit who can collect wafer-scale serial sections for connectomics.
ocar.action: Medina, Gogola, Wildenberg and colleagues (Cell Reports Methods, 2026) introduce DRIFT-EM (direct retrieval by ionizer-facilitated transfer): off-the-shelf static ionizers clear sections from the knife, a thermoplastic boundary confines them on silicon wafers, 3D-printed parts complete the boat, and open-source software maps regions of interest.
ocar.resolution: They report section packing densities comparable to established magnetic methods with minimal setup cost and maintenance, and they frame the platform as modular and complementary to tape- and magnet-based systems. ROI scripts currently emit Zeiss ATLAS-compatible XML.
ocar.future_work: The authors list practical limits—ionizer geometry tuning, barrier dexterity, machine-shop knife modification, and untested ports to non-ATLAS SEM software—and invite community STL and software variants.

summaries.beginner: Making a big electron-microscope map of a brain requires collecting thousands of extremely thin slices, which usually needs expensive special gear. This team shows a cheaper way to float those slices onto silicon wafers using ordinary static ionizers, 3D-printed parts, and open software.
summaries.intermediate: Medina, Gogola et al. (Cell Reports Methods, 2026) present DRIFT-EM, a low-cost wafer-collection method for ultrathin serial sections. Static ionizers clear sections from the knife edge, a thermoplastic barrier confines them, and a Python ROI-mapping pipeline guides automated imaging. They report packing densities comparable to magnetic collectors (MagC-style) while using commonly available and 3D-printed components, and they position DRIFT-EM as complementary to ATUM tape collection and magnet-based systems. The accompanying scripts currently write Zeiss ATLAS XML.
summaries.advanced: This is an accessibility and methods paper, not a new reconstructed connectome. ‘Comparable packing density’ is the headline quantitative claim in the selected text; error rates, section loss, or downstream segmentation quality versus ATUM/MagC are not the focus of the summary extract. Integration still needs a machine shop for knife modification, empirical ionizer placement, and ATLAS-oriented ROI output unless users port the XML. The authors treat these as practical rather than conceptual limits.

plain_language_summary: Making a big electron-microscope map of a brain requires collecting thousands of extremely thin slices, which usually needs expensive special gear. This team shows a cheaper way to float those slices onto silicon wafers using ordinary static ionizers, 3D-printed parts, and open software.

ocar.opportunity: A dense Male Adult Nerve Cord (MANC) connectome makes it possible, for the first time at synaptic resolution, to ask how descending brain neurons reach motor neurons in the fly ventral nerve cord.
ocar.challenge: Direct brain-to-muscle paths are expected to be rare, but the community organization of walking, flight, and mixed wing–leg control has not been surveyed at this scale.
ocar.action: Cheong, Eichler, Stürner, Jefferis, Card and colleagues (eLife, 2026) proofread and curate all descending neurons (DNs) and motor neurons (MNs), match morphologies to light microscopy, and analyze DN-to-MN networks using companion MANC connectivity and lineage papers.
ocar.resolution: They count 1328 DNs (above prior estimates of 700–1100), 1864 ascending neurons, and 737 MNs, and they match 29% of DNs and 55% of MNs to light-level identities. Direct DN–MN connections are infrequent (typically <10% of MN input synapses), though about 80% of MN groups receive some direct DN input at a 1% threshold; neck and some abdominal MNs are outliers with DN input up to 60%. Anatomical DN subclasses target dorsal, ventral, or mixed neuropils, including walking, flight steering/power, and coordinated wing–leg communities.
ocar.future_work: Unmatched DN and MN types remain to be linked at the light level; the authors treat the maps as hypotheses for physiology and as a resource for others to query VNC circuits.

summaries.beginner: To move, a fly’s brain must talk to motor neurons in the nerve cord, but those paths are hard to see. Using a complete male nerve-cord wiring map, this team shows that brain cells rarely plug straight into muscles and instead work through communities that look like walking, flight, and mixed wing–leg control.
summaries.intermediate: Cheong, Eichler, Stürner et al. (eLife, 2026), with Jefferis and Card as corresponding authors, analyze the Drosophila Male Adult Nerve Cord connectome of Takemura et al. (2024) and cell-type/lineage annotations of Marin et al. (2024). After proofreading all DNs and MNs, they report 1328 DNs, 1864 ascending neurons, and 737 MNs, with 29% of DNs and 55% of MNs matched to light microscopy. Direct DN input to most MNs is low (<10% of input synapses), yet ~80% of MN groups receive some direct DN input at a 1% threshold, with neck and some abdominal MNs as high-input outliers. They propose a systematic DN nomenclature by target neuropil and identify communities putatively tied to walking, flight, and coordinated wing–leg action.
summaries.advanced: eLife assessment calls the evidence solid and the work important as a hypothesis generator, not a functional proof. Light-level matches cover only 29% of DNs and 55% of MNs. Motor-system labels for communities are inferred from anatomy and connectivity, not from simultaneous behavior or physiology in this paper. Direct-connection percentages depend on chosen synapse-input thresholds. The reconstruction is male VNC; comparison to female nerve cord is left to companion comparative work.

plain_language_summary: To move, a fly’s brain must talk to motor neurons in the nerve cord, but those paths are hard to see. Using a complete male nerve-cord wiring map, this team shows that brain cells rarely plug straight into muscles and instead work through communities that look like walking, flight, and mixed wing–leg control.

ocar.opportunity: Many neurons mix presynaptic and postsynaptic sites on the same arbor, so a complete brain connectome can ask how often wiring is not simply axon-to-dendrite.
ocar.challenge: Non-canonical synapse types (axo-axonic, dendrodendritic, dendro-axonic) are known in selected circuits, but their brain-wide organization has not been quantified.
ocar.action: Gross, Farah, Jana, Dorkenwald, Bock, and Deutsch (bioRxiv, 2026) map synapse types across compartments, cell types, and regions in an adult Drosophila brain connectome of approximately 140,000 neurons and more than 80 million synapses.
ocar.resolution: Mixed polarity is widespread but structured: about one third of synapses between polarized neurons are non-canonical. Synapse type is predictable from a morphology-and-connectivity complexity axis—low-complexity early visual neurons interact more through dendrites, larger highly connected central neurons more through axons. Mixed polarity promotes reciprocal connectivity dominated by non-canonical motifs, and postsynaptic terminals on presynaptic boutons are a common local motif.
ocar.future_work: How these anatomical rules translate to physiology, and whether they hold in other complete brains, is left open; the preprint cites emerging CNS and vertebrate volumes as natural tests.

summaries.beginner: Textbooks say dendrites take messages in and axons send them out, but many neurons mix both on the same branches. Using a complete fly-brain wiring map, this team shows that mixed wiring is common, follows simple complexity rules, and often makes two-way connections.
summaries.intermediate: Gross et al. (bioRxiv, 2026) classify synapse types across the complete adult Drosophila brain connectome (~140,000 neurons, >80 million synapses). About one third of synapses between polarized neurons are non-canonical (axo-axonic, dendrodendritic, or dendro-axonic). A simple neuronal-complexity axis from morphology and connectivity predicts synapse type: low-complexity neurons that dominate early vision prefer dendritic interactions, whereas larger, more connected central-brain neurons prefer axonal interactions. Mixed polarity strongly promotes reciprocal connectivity, and postsynaptic terminals on presynaptic boutons emerge as a widespread local motif. The paper is a whole-brain anatomical census, not a new EM acquisition.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. ‘Polarized’ versus mixed-polarity labels depend on how axonal and dendritic compartments are assigned in the reconstruction. The one-third non-canonical figure is for synapses between polarized neurons, not all synapses. Complexity-axis prediction is correlative. Reciprocal and bouton-terminal motifs are structural; inhibitory versus excitatory function is not resolved from synapse-type geometry alone here.

plain_language_summary: Textbooks say dendrites take messages in and axons send them out, but many neurons mix both on the same branches. Using a complete fly-brain wiring map, this team shows that mixed wiring is common, follows simple complexity rules, and often makes two-way connections.

ocar.opportunity: The insect neck connective is a physical and information bottleneck of descending, ascending, and sensory-ascending neurons, so a complete synaptic map would show how brain and nerve cord talk during behavior, including sex-specific acts.
ocar.challenge: Those neurons are split across separate EM volumes, sexes, and light-level driver libraries, so matching types has been incomplete.
ocar.action: Stürner, Brooks, Jefferis, Eichler and colleagues (Nature, 2025) integrate three EM datasets to reconstruct female descending and ascending neurons, compare them to the male nerve cord, match types across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes, link 51% of DN cell types to light-level driver lines, and classify all ascending populations.
ocar.resolution: They report connected DN–AN chains spanning the neck that may support motor sequences, and they give complete sexually dimorphic DN/AN descriptions with circuit analyses of male courtship (DNa12/aSP22), song (hemilineage 08B ascending neurons), and female ovipositor extrusion (DNp13). Early data access already supported locomotor and DN logic studies; Neuroglancer scenes are transformed into male CNS space.
ocar.future_work: Forthcoming full-CNS datasets are needed to close remaining truncation and matching gaps; the authors argue that rigorous cross-dataset type matching, including sexual dimorphism definitions, will be essential as more specimens appear.

summaries.beginner: A fly’s brain and body are linked by a thin neck cable of neurons that send commands down and senses back up. This Nature paper stitches three electron-microscope maps to finish that cable in the female, compare it with the male, and tie many cell types to genetic tools used in experiments.
summaries.intermediate: Stürner et al. (Nature, 2025) combine three EM volumes to give a complete connectomic description of descending neurons (DNs), ascending neurons (ANs), and sensory ascending neurons in the Drosophila female nervous system, matched to the male nerve cord. Proofread reconstructions are matched across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes; 51% of DN cell types are linked to light-level driver lines, and all ascending populations are classified. They describe DN–AN chains spanning the neck and analyze sexually dimorphic circuits for courtship (DNa12/aSP22), song (08B ANs), and ovipositor extrusion (DNp13). The work supplies EM-level analyses spanning the adult central nervous system rather than a single neuropil.
summaries.advanced: Sample size remains small (a handful of EM specimens), a limitation the authors themselves emphasize even while using more datasets than typical single-volume studies. 51% of DN types—not all—are matched to driver lines. Functional labels (courtship, song, oviposition) rest on prior genetics plus new connectivity, not new physiology in this paper. Truncation and cross-alignment issues persist until full-CNS volumes; male–female comparisons inherit those matching uncertainties.

plain_language_summary: A fly’s brain and body are linked by a thin neck cable of neurons that send commands down and senses back up. This Nature paper stitches three electron-microscope maps to finish that cable in the female, compare it with the male, and tie many cell types to genetic tools used in experiments.

ocar.opportunity: Fly visual neuropils occupy a huge fraction of the brain and have century-old cell-type catalogs, but a complete synaptic inventory plus genetic drivers would let anatomy, transmitters, and experiments share one list.
ocar.challenge: Cell-type diversity, spatial maps, and structure–function links are hard to unify without a dense EM reconstruction matched to light-level tools.
ocar.action: Nern, Loesche, Takemura, Berg, Rubin, Reiser and colleagues (Nature, 2025) acquire a focused-ion-beam SEM connectome of the right optic lobe of a male Drosophila melanogaster, quantify anatomy computationally, and classify approximately 53,000 neurons into 732 types using connectivity, predicted transmitters, and expert curation, about half of them newly named, while sharing matched split-GAL4 lines.
ocar.resolution: The inventory is designed so neuronal shape can be read in terms of spatial vision, and types are systematically described. Cross-matching to FlyWire uses NBLAST in a common space plus morphology review (and connectivity for hard ONIN/ONCN cases); 170 of 732 types have unclear transmitter predictions under a conservative consensus policy, 132 of those being visual projection neurons.
ocar.future_work: Most split-GAL4 images are female while the EM volume is male; the authors report nearly every type still matches, with one stated exception, and they treat remaining unclear transmitters and untyped candidates as open matching work.

summaries.beginner: Half of a fly’s brain is for seeing, with an enormous variety of cell types. This team mapped the right visual lobe of a male fruit fly in an electron microscope, named hundreds of types—many for the first time—and matched them to genetic tools so labs can turn those cells on and off.
summaries.intermediate: Nern et al. (Nature, 2025) present a FIB-SEM connectome of the right optic lobe of a male Drosophila melanogaster. Combining quantitative anatomy, connectivity, neurotransmitter prediction, and expert curation, they classify about 53,000 neurons into 732 types, systematically described, with about half newly named, and they release an extensive split-GAL4 collection matched to that catalog. Cross-dataset matching to FlyWire uses bidirectional NBLAST after transforming optic-lobe skeletons into FAFB space, followed by independent morphological review. Conservative consensus transmitter calls leave 170 types unclear (132 VPNs). The resource is meant as a foundation for systematic visual physiology and modeling.
summaries.advanced: Completeness caveats include male EM versus mostly female light-level driver images, with one unmatched exception noted. Transmitter identity is predicted, not biochemically confirmed; 170 types remain unclear. Some groups (ONIN, ONCN) are hard to distinguish by morphology alone and needed connectivity clustering. Counts and names are for this optic-lobe release (neuPrint optic-lobe:v1.0.1 in the matching methods) and may differ from hemibrain/FlyWire naming without the provided crosswalks.

plain_language_summary: Half of a fly’s brain is for seeing, with an enormous variety of cell types. This team mapped the right visual lobe of a male fruit fly in an electron microscope, named hundreds of types—many for the first time—and matched them to genetic tools so labs can turn those cells on and off.

ocar.opportunity: Light microscopy can show specific molecules, but dense synapse-level circuit reconstruction has been an electron-microscopy specialty because diffraction-limited light cannot separate packed neurites.
ocar.challenge: Resolution, contrast, and volumetric imaging have kept light-based dense connectomics out of reach, so molecular identity and full wiring are usually collected in different experiments.
ocar.action: Tavakoli, Lyudchik, Januszewski, Danzl and colleagues (Nature, 2025) introduce LICONN (light-microscopy-based connectomics): engineered hydrogel embedding and expansion plus deep-learning segmentation and connectivity analysis, demonstrated on mammalian brain tissue including thick hippocampal CA1 slices and multi-round block-face imaging.
ocar.resolution: They argue LICONN can incorporate molecular information directly into synapse-level reconstructions and will allow synapse-level phenotyping in a more adoptable optical workflow. Extended data illustrate iterative imaging/sectioning of expanded hydrogel (for example two-round fusion of a 6×6×2 grid and a 3×3×12 grid whose fused axial extent is 205 µm at original tissue scale).
ocar.future_work: The authors present LICONN as enabling biological experiments rather than as a finished whole-brain mammalian connectome; scaling, tracing completeness, and molecular multiplexing limits remain the practical next tests.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can map every connection, but they do not easily show which molecules sit at those connections. This team expands brain tissue in a gel, images it with light, and uses machine learning to trace cells and synapses while keeping molecular labels.
summaries.intermediate: Tavakoli et al. (Nature, 2025) describe LICONN, integrating hydrogel expansion with deep-learning segmentation so light microscopy can reconstruct densely labeled mammalian neuropil at synapse level and attach molecular information to those reconstructions. Conventional light resolution (best-case hundreds of nanometres laterally, often ~1 µm axially) is treated as too coarse for dense tracing; expansion plus computational segmentation is the proposed route. Extended data show multi-tile, multi-round block-face imaging of expanded CA1 tissue with seamless fusion, including a fused volume of 205 µm original-tissue axial extent from 12 imaging rounds. The claim is adoptable synapse-level phenotyping, not replacement of all EM connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is not a whole-brain mammalian connectome. Expansion factor, residual distortion, and automated versus manual tracing completeness should be read from the full figures rather than assumed from the slogan. Molecular incorporation is a design goal of the hydrogel/labeling strategy; the selected extract does not quantify how many molecular channels survive expansion at connectomic density. Comparison with EM error rates on the same tissue is the natural external benchmark and is not fully settled by the front matter alone.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can map every connection, but they do not easily show which molecules sit at those connections. This team expands brain tissue in a gel, images it with light, and uses machine learning to trace cells and synapses while keeping molecular labels.

ocar.opportunity: Brain-wide activity maps, connectomes, and cell atlases now exist for C. elegans and Drosophila, so structure and function can be compared at nervous-system scale rather than one circuit at a time.
ocar.challenge: How activity is coordinated across regions, and which structural motifs must enter whole-brain models, remains open even in these small animals.
ocar.action: Kramer and Flavell (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2024) review recent whole-brain calcium imaging in behaving worms and flies, maps of connectivity, transmitter/receptor identity, and neuromodulation, and circuit motifs with known structure–function links, largely from the past few years.
ocar.resolution: C. elegans now has an atlas of how most neurons encode spontaneous behavior, and Drosophila activity maps give a global view of dynamics, alongside genetic and synaptic maps in both species. The authors argue that flexibility, degeneracy, extrasynaptic signaling, and receptor kinetics are still missing ingredients for accurate whole-brain models.
ocar.future_work: They call for brain-wide recordings across behavioral states and motivated contexts, large-scale views of transmitter and neuropeptide dynamics, and models that generate testable predictions rather than assuming fixed activity maps.

summaries.beginner: For tiny animals like worms and fruit flies, scientists can now record almost the whole brain while the animal moves, and they also have wiring diagrams. This review asks how to put those maps together so we can explain real behavior, not just one circuit at a time.
summaries.intermediate: Kramer and Flavell (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2024) review brain-wide maps of structure and function in C. elegans and Drosophila. They cover whole-brain calcium imaging in immobilized and freely moving animals, connectomes, genetic identity, and neuromodulation, then walk through circuit motifs that show why whole-brain models must capture more than a static wiring diagram. They note that C. elegans has an atlas of how most neurons encode spontaneous behavior, while fly activity maps provide a global dynamical view, and that both species now have synaptic and receptor/transmitter maps. Mammalian brain-wide imaging is treated as still incomplete despite recordings of over a million mouse cortical neurons.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a primary reconstruction or a new activity dataset. Species parallels are suggestive, not proof of shared algorithms. The authors explicitly say current activity maps will not be fixed across states. Citations to ‘most neurons’ in the worm atlas and to million-neuron mouse cortex are pointers to other papers; readers should not treat this article as the source of those measurements.

plain_language_summary: For tiny animals like worms and fruit flies, scientists can now record almost the whole brain while the animal moves, and they also have wiring diagrams. This review asks how to put those maps together so we can explain real behavior, not just one circuit at a time.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale EM and X-ray micro/holographic-nano tomography volumes are multiplying across species, regions, and techniques, and shared metadata would make comparative connectomics and software interoperability realistic.
ocar.challenge: Neuroinformatics standards that work for other modalities have not covered EM and XRM/XHN connectomics, so datasets remain isolated with idiosyncratic metadata.
ocar.action: Wimbish, Guittari, Rose, Johnson, Gray-Roncal and the BENCHMARK working group (arXiv preprint, version 1.1 dated December 30, 2025 in the PDF) specify Image and Experimental Metadata Standards for EM and XRM/XHN, including classes such as contributors, license, funder, projects, taxonomy, coordinate frame, publication, and links, with a companion document for derived annotations.
ocar.resolution: The document is a community standard (v1.1) intended to support metadata services and future software, with definitions on a community GitHub page and an acronym table covering ATUM-SEM, FIB-SEM, SB-SEM, XRM, and identifier schemes (ORCID, RRID, ROR, and others).
ocar.future_work: The authors hope the standards will be refined by the community; adoption, not a new dataset, is the measure of success.

summaries.beginner: Giant microscope maps of brains are hard to compare if every lab describes the experiment differently. This working-group paper proposes shared labels for how electron-microscope and X-ray volumes were made, so the files can be found, combined, and reused.
summaries.intermediate: Wimbish et al. (arXiv, BENCHMARK standards v1.1) present imaging and experimental metadata standards for electron microscopy and X-ray micro / holographic-nano tomography connectomics. They argue that FAIR-style standardization, already common in other neuroinformatics modalities, has not reached these volumetric datasets. Version 1.1 defines required and optional fields (contributors, license, taxonomy, coordinate frame, publication, links, and others) to support metadata services; annotation standards are deferred to a companion document. A stakeholder working group is listed, and technique abbreviations span ATUM-SEM, FIB-SEM, serial block-face SEM, TEM variants, and XRM.
summaries.advanced: This is a standards preprint, not a validation that labs have adopted the schema. Many fields in the excerpted table are optional. Interoperability gains depend on uptake by repositories and tools. The selected extract is partly a field dictionary; it does not benchmark completeness of metadata on existing public volumes.

plain_language_summary: Giant microscope maps of brains are hard to compare if every lab describes the experiment differently. This working-group paper proposes shared labels for how electron-microscope and X-ray volumes were made, so the files can be found, combined, and reused.

ocar.opportunity: Volume-EM connectomes contain not only synapses but also cell-biological contacts that can be compared across developmental stages if graph analytics stay linked to the underlying anatomy.
ocar.challenge: High-dimensional adjacency and contact measurements are hard to inspect without a platform that moves between abstract graphs and neuropil features.
ocar.action: Koonce, Emerson, Colón-Ramos, Mohler and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2024; version posted May 27, 2025) introduce NeuroSC/NeuroSCAN, an open-source online platform, and apply it to a series of published C. elegans brain neuropils spanning larval stages through adult.
ocar.resolution: Integrated graphical representations of neuronal relationships are used to compare connectomes and to prompt structure–function and developmental insights. Supplemental adjacency tables quantify contacts and pixel-weighted adjacencies at L1 (5 h post hatching), L2 (23 h), L3 (27 h), L4 (36 h), and adult (48 h).
ocar.future_work: The platform is framed as a way to keep synthesizing abstractions with cell-biological detail as more staged connectomes appear.

summaries.beginner: Worm brains have been mapped at several ages, but the tables of who touches whom are hard to browse. This team built a website that lets you jump from a simplified graph of neuron relationships down to the actual cell contacts that change as the worm grows.
summaries.intermediate: Koonce, Emerson et al. (bioRxiv, 2024) present NeuroSC (also called NeuroSCAN), an open-source platform linking data-science graph views of neuronal relationships to cell-biological features in volume-EM connectomes. They analyze published C. elegans brain neuropils across development and argue that these integrated representations make cross-connectome comparison tractable. Supplemental resources include searchable adjacency counts (number of EM sections in contact and summed pixel weights) for L1 through adult, with times such as 5, 23, 27, 36, and 48 hours post hatching. The contribution is visualization and collation infrastructure plus developmental comparison, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint methods/resource paper on published worm neuropils. Insights into structure–function are catalyzed by the representations; they are not independently validated with new physiology here. Adjacency is contact in EM sections, which is not identical to synaptic connectivity. Users should check which published reconstructions and neuropil masks feed each stage table.

plain_language_summary: Worm brains have been mapped at several ages, but the tables of who touches whom are hard to browse. This team built a website that lets you jump from a simplified graph of neuron relationships down to the actual cell contacts that change as the worm grows.

ocar.opportunity: A whole-animal scanning transmission EM volume of Drosophila can, in principle, map every gut–brain path through the insect vagus at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: How the body tells the brain that swallowing succeeded, and how serotonin then values that act, has not been reconstructed as a complete circuit.
ocar.action: Schoofs, Miroschnikow, Pankratz and colleagues (Current Biology, 2024) reconstruct enteric-to-brain circuits in a whole-larva STEM volume and combine that anatomy with functional arguments about Piezo mechanosensors and serotonergic modulation.
ocar.resolution: Piezo-expressing esophageal mechanosensory neurons (EGpost on the myogenic esophagus) report food passage to a cluster of six central serotonergic neurons, which, together with food-value information, enhance serotonin-receptor-7 motor neurons that drive swallowing. Glutamatergic esophageal motor neurons make axo-axonic synapses onto those mechanosensors. The authors interpret this as a neuromodulatory loop that strengthens ongoing swallowing when a biologically meaningful act is completed, possibly an ancient form of motor learning.
ocar.future_work: They separate ‘mission accomplished’ sensing, value encoding, and reinforcement as conceptual questions still to be tested beyond this larval swallowing system.

summaries.beginner: Swallowing is the moment food is truly taken in, but how the gut tells the brain ‘that worked’ is usually guessed, not wired out. Using a whole-larva fly electron-microscope map, this team finds stretch sensors in the esophagus that talk to six serotonin cells, which then boost the motor neurons that swallow.
summaries.intermediate: Schoofs et al. (Current Biology, 2024) map the Drosophila enteric nervous system’s links to the brain via the insect vagus in a whole-animal STEM volume. They describe a feedback loop: Piezo-positive esophageal mechanosensors, especially EGpost on the myogenic esophagus, signal completed food passage to six serotonergic brain neurons that modulate 5-HT7 motor neurons. An axo-axonic synapse from glutamatergic esophageal motor neurons onto the mechanosensors is part of the architecture. Discussion contrasts neurogenic initiation at the pharynx–esophagus junction with myogenic peristalsis and treats EGpost as a ‘mission accomplished’ sensor rather than a deglutition trigger. Anatomy is paired with the claim that serotonin reinforces high-value completed swallows.
summaries.advanced: The volume is larval Drosophila, not adult. Piezo expression and activity-during-feeding arguments support the stretch hypothesis but do not fully substitute for in vivo force measurements in the selected text. The ‘ancient motor learning’ framing is interpretive. Completeness claims refer to feeding-relevant body–brain connections in this STEM volume; they should not be read as a complete adult autonomic connectome.

Using a whole-larva fly electron-microscope map, this team finds stretch sensors in the esophagus that talk to six serotonin cells, which then boost the motor neurons that swallow.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic EM volumes reach tera- to petascale with appearance that shifts by sample preparation, so synapse detectors must work when labeled training data are a tiny fraction of the volume.
ocar.challenge: Domain-adaptation methods are common in natural images but lacked a public synapse-detection benchmark on biological EM domains.
ocar.action: Li, Wu, Wei, Pfister and colleagues (IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, 2024) annotated 14 volumes from biologically diverse Megaphragma viggianii brain regions across three whole-brain datasets and ran the WASPSYN challenge at ISBI 2023, with 3D pre- and postsynaptic coordinates plus one-to-many connectivity, a two-step baseline, and CodaLab evaluation.
ocar.resolution: The paper reports the dataset, tasks, baseline, evaluation, challenge results, and limitations. The challenge remains open at the CodaLab URL given in the text. Ground-truth annotators and imaging (Pang and Xu in the Hess lab at Janelia) are acknowledged.
ocar.future_work: The authors hope winning algorithms will generalize to real-world connectomics; they discuss challenge limits and neuroscience impact rather than declaring a solved detector.

summaries.beginner: Computers that find synapses in brain pictures often fail when the next sample was prepared a little differently. This team labeled synapses in tiny wasp brains from three different datasets and ran a public contest so methods can be compared fairly when the pictures change.
summaries.intermediate: Li et al. (IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, 2024) describe WASPSYN, an ISBI 2023 challenge for domain-adaptive synapse detection in Megaphragma viggianii. Fourteen annotated EM volumes from three whole-brain samples provide pre- and postsynaptic 3D coordinates and one-to-many connectivity. Labeled training data in typical connectomics applications are described as often smaller than 0.001% of the target volume, motivating out-of-domain evaluation. A two-step baseline, public starter code, and online CodaLab scoring (https://codalab.lisn.upsaclay.fr/competitions/9169) are provided. Imaging and alignment were done by Pang and Xu in Harald Hess’s Janelia lab.
summaries.advanced: This is a benchmark and challenge report, not a claim that domain shift is solved. The 0.001% figure characterizes the general labeling problem, not necessarily the fraction labeled in these 14 volumes. Success on microwasp appearance shift may not transfer to mammalian EM. One-to-many connectivity annotations add task richness but also annotation noise risk; the paper discusses limitations of the challenge design.

plain_language_summary: Computers that find synapses in brain pictures often fail when the next sample was prepared a little differently. This team labeled synapses in tiny wasp brains from three different datasets and ran a public contest so methods can be compared fairly when the pictures change.

ocar.opportunity: The microinsect Megaphragma viggianii is small enough for whole-head electron microscopy while still flying, so its early visual system could expose a minimal flying-insect circuit.
ocar.challenge: Most neuroscience model species lack a complete high-resolution map of the compound eye and first visual neuropil, which blocks compact computational models of insect vision.
ocar.action: Chua, Polilov, Chklovskii and colleagues (Current Biology, 2023), as described in the catalog abstract, image the whole head with serial EM, reconstruct the compound eye, analyze ommatidial optics, and reconstruct the lamina connectome.
ocar.resolution: Relative to fruit fly and honeybee, the visual system is highly simplified: 29 ommatidia per eye and 6 lamina neuron types, with both stereotyped and specialized ommatidial features. The authors argue this ‘barebones’ flying-insect circuit will aid computational models of visual processing.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the reconstruction as a substrate for models; how specializations map onto behavior is left to subsequent analysis.

summaries.beginner: Some tiny wasps have very small eyes but can still fly, which makes them a good place to look for the simplest flying visual circuit. This paper maps one such wasp’s eye and the first brain station behind it, finding only 29 facets per eye and six cell types in that first station.
summaries.intermediate: Chua et al. (Current Biology, 2023) reconstruct the early visual system of adult Megaphragma viggianii from whole-head serial electron microscopy. They analyze ommatidial optics and the lamina connectome, reporting 29 ommatidia per eye and six lamina neuron types—far simpler than Drosophila or honeybee. Features that are shared across most ommatidia are distinguished from specialized ones. The stated goal is to identify circuits critical for flying insects and to facilitate computational models. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is a 2026 Insects review by Varone et al. on pest-management applications of insect vision, not the Chua et al. reconstruction; numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Current Biology paper is needed for methods, error rates, and figures. Do not treat the Varone review’s pest-trap discussion as part of this work.

plain_language_summary: Some tiny wasps have very small eyes but can still fly, which makes them a good place to look for the simplest flying visual circuit. This paper maps one such wasp’s eye and the first brain station behind it, finding only 29 facets per eye and six cell types in that first station.

ocar.opportunity: False splits at neurite tips hide many synapses from their parent cell, so cheap geometric flags for those tips could speed both human and automated extension.
ocar.challenge: Manual proofreading of petascale EM segmentations is still required, and existing extension tools do not first cheaply rank likely error locations.
ocar.action: Joyce, Chalavadi, Chan, Tanna, Wester and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2023) use mesh processing to find likely errors near neuronal tips and embed that detector in a semi-automated proofreading pipeline, including an attempt at fully automated extension seeded by those endpoints using Sofima optical flow.
ocar.resolution: Guiding proofreaders to flagged locations improved average edit rate even with loading-time overhead. Fully automated extension often chose the correct candidate but struggled when more than three consecutive slices were blacked out or when misalignments were large.
ocar.future_work: They suggest adding geometric features or machine learning for higher-precision localization, cutting UI loading time, and using GAN or other large models where alignment fails.

summaries.beginner: When a computer map of a neuron is cut off too early, many of that cell’s connections are missing. This team looks at the shape of those dead ends, points proofreaders at the likely breaks, and shows that people fix mistakes faster when they are pointed in the right direction.
summaries.intermediate: Joyce et al. (bioRxiv, 2023; JHU APL) detect likely false splits near tips of EM neuron meshes and route those locations into a semi-automated proofreading workflow aimed at neurite extension. They motivate the problem with hemibrain- and MICrONS-scale volumes and contrast the approach with tools such as RoboEM and NEURD. In their implementation, proofreader efficiency (edit rate) rose when tasks were oriented to predicted error sites, despite loading delays between tasks. A fully automated extension attempt using mesh-based Sofima optical flow often selected the correct continuation but failed on stretches with more than three blacked-out slices or large misalignments.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint methods paper. The selected text does not give a single headline accuracy percentage for the tip detector. Automated extension is explicitly not robust to severe missing-section and misalignment artifacts. Results depend on the segmentation and alignment quality of the host volume (MICrONS-related in the funding and introduction). Improving loading time is acknowledged as a confounder of human-rate measurements.

plain_language_summary: When a computer map of a neuron is cut off too early, many of that cell’s connections are missing. This team looks at the shape of those dead ends, points proofreaders at the likely breaks, and shows that people fix mistakes faster when they are pointed in the right direction.

ocar.opportunity: EM wiring diagrams invite cross-species comparison of sensorimotor organization, using C. elegans feedforwardness as the classic foil.
ocar.challenge: Whether vertebrate circuits show the opposite—overrepresented cellular cycles—had not been shown in any EM connectome.
ocar.action: Yang, Vishwanathan, Wu, Aksay, Seung and colleagues (Current Biology, 2023) analyze a larval zebrafish brainstem wiring diagram, focusing on the oculomotor module, counting three-cell cycles against feedforward loops (U3 and C3), and fitting a stochastic block model.
ocar.resolution: Three-cycles are highly overrepresented, a first among EM neuronal wiring diagrams they survey. Cellular cycles align with a three-cycle of neuronal groups in the SBM but are more specific than group structure can explain, with surprisingly common recurrence to the same neuron. Most three-cycles lack inhibitory Ve2 cells and are therefore expected to be all-excitatory. The cyclic structure coexists with the classic horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex arc and is discussed in light of recurrent integrator models.
ocar.future_work: The functional meaning of cellular (not just group) specificity remains unclear; the authors note that a three-block cycle would already suffice for positive feedback.

summaries.beginner: Worm wiring is often described as a one-way path from sensors to muscles. In a young zebrafish eye-movement circuit, this team instead finds many three-cell loops, including loops that return to the same cell, which may help the brain hold a signal over time.
summaries.intermediate: Yang et al. (Current Biology, 2023) contrast the feedforward C. elegans sensorimotor connectome with a larval zebrafish brainstem reconstruction. In the oculomotor module, the three-cycle motif is highly overrepresented relative to feedforward loops, reported as a first for EM wiring diagrams (invertebrate or mammalian) in their comparison set. Cycles align with a three-group cycle in a stochastic block model but show extra cellular specificity. Bidirectional connections are less overrepresented than in C. elegans, consistent with mostly axodendritic synapses that do not invite nearby reciprocal contacts. Registration to Z-Brain gene expression had previously suggested most module cells are excitatory except Ve2.
summaries.advanced: Comparing an entire worm connectome to one zebrafish module is a principled but coarse analogy, which the authors defend at the level of general organization rather than cell homology. Motif overrepresentation depends on the null model (they discuss CFG versus ER). Excitatory-loop inference uses atlas registration plus Ve2 as the inhibitory exception, not paired physiology. Whether cycles implement a neural integrator is a theoretical link, not a causal test in this report.

plain_language_summary: Worm wiring is often described as a one-way path from sensors to muscles. In a young zebrafish eye-movement circuit, this team instead finds many three-cell loops, including loops that return to the same cell, which may help the brain hold a signal over time.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes are usually one-of-a-kind, so discovering repeated subgraphs cannot wait for large samples of host graphs, and exhaustive subgraph search is intractable.
ocar.challenge: Standard motif tests can mislead if the random-graph null is wrong, and listing all subgraphs does not scale.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Robinette, Wester, Gray-Roncal, Johnson, and Reilly (bioRxiv, 2023) propose improved randomization for significance, a progressive-refinement discovery procedure for directed or undirected motifs from a single graph, sampling corrections, and an open-source Python package, demonstrated on the C. elegans connectome and the Drosophila ellipsoid body.
ocar.resolution: They show that standard random-graph models can produce misleading significance calls, that their sampling correction supports testing of target motifs, and that discovered motifs include biologically familiar recurrence, feedback, and feedforward loops. Code, data, and infrastructure—including unsuccessful forays—are released for reuse.
ocar.future_work: Whether motifs are conserved across individuals, how to separate core from periphery, and how structure maps to attractor dynamics are posed as community-scale next questions.

summaries.beginner: Scientists want to know which small wiring patterns repeat in a brain map, but each map is usually one of a kind and too big to search blindly. This team offers a method and open software to find those patterns in a single connectome and to test whether they are really unusual.
summaries.intermediate: Matelsky et al. (bioRxiv, 2023) tackle data-driven motif discovery on single biological graphs. They critique common statistical pitfalls in motif enrichment, propose better randomization, and use progressive refinement to control computational cost while returning directed or undirected motifs with counts versus randomized graphs. Preliminary demonstrations use the C. elegans connectome and the ellipsoid body of Drosophila. An open-source Python package is provided. The discussion treats familiar motif classes (recurrence, feedforward/feedback) as expected and asks whether they are conserved across individuals.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint methods paper with ‘preliminary’ biological results. Enrichment is always relative to the chosen null; the authors’ point is that naive nulls mislead, so readers should inspect which generator was used. Discovery on one C. elegans graph and one fly subnetwork does not establish species-wide conservation. Functional interpretation of motifs is explicitly deferred.

plain_language_summary: Scientists want to know which small wiring patterns repeat in a brain map, but each map is usually one of a kind and too big to search blindly. This team offers a method and open software to find those patterns in a single connectome and to test whether they are really unusual.

ocar.opportunity: Fully automatic 3D instance segmentation of EM still fails on thin processes, so labs need a way to sketch neurons quickly and let a network clean the shapes.
ocar.challenge: Even painstaking proofreading leaves small errors, and marker-based 2-D region growing on EM has lagged other instance-segmentation settings.
ocar.action: Chen, Bangalore Renuka, Mi, Lichtman, Shavit, and Meirovitch (CVPR Workshops, 2023) introduce EMProof, learning to shrink and expand sloppy manual annotations via a marker-based 2-D instance segmentation network, tested on public benchmarks, large-scale neuron problems, a new octopus dataset, and a super-resolution setting on mouse cortex AC3.
ocar.resolution: They report near-ground-truth morphology while cutting annotation time about 8× on several connectomics examples, a new state of the art among region-growing algorithms on challenging EM stacks, and, on AC3, 16-fold XY super-resolution from coarse low-resolution segmentation with a majority of regions reaching VI under 0.04 and many improvement factors of 4–8×. Architecture ablations (U-Net plus hypercolumns, two-branch, and the full proposed model) are tabulated on skeletal inputs.
ocar.future_work: They suggest the same primitive may apply to other reconstruction tasks where a coarse human sketch is refined by learning.

summaries.beginner: Drawing every neuron perfectly in electron-microscope pictures is slow, so people often sketch roughly. This team trains a network to tidy those sloppy sketches into accurate shapes, cutting tracing time on several examples and even working from blurrier, lower-resolution pictures.
summaries.intermediate: Chen et al. (CVPRW, 2023) present EMProof, which takes imperfect instance annotations—skeletons or tiny seeds—and learns to correct them by shrinking and expanding objects. They claim state-of-the-art among region-growing methods on hard EM stacks and about an 8× annotation-time reduction on several connectomics examples, including an octopus volume they say existing automatic segmenters cannot handle at scale. On the AC3 mouse-cortex benchmark, coarse low-resolution segmentations are super-resolved 16-fold in X and Y, with a large fraction of the data showing 4–8× VI improvement and most achieving VI under 0.04. The framework is 2-D marker-based instance segmentation used to accelerate manual 3-D reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Headline 8× time savings are for ‘several examples,’ not a universal multiplier. VI under 0.04 and 16-fold super-resolution are AC3-specific. The octopus claim is that existing algorithms cannot automatically segment that dataset at scale; it is not a public leaderboard win against all later methods. EMProof addresses morphological reconstruction quality, not synapse graph correctness by itself. Funding from Thermo Fisher is disclosed.

plain_language_summary: Drawing every neuron perfectly in electron-microscope pictures is slow, so people often sketch roughly. This team trains a network to tidy those sloppy sketches into accurate shapes, cutting tracing time on several examples and even working from blurrier, lower-resolution pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila now has dense CNS connectomes, transcriptomes, and huge driver-line image libraries, so a FAIR atlas could let researchers find neurons, reagents, and citations in one place.
ocar.challenge: The data are scattered across modalities and databases, making integrated hypothesis generation and reagent choice difficult.
ocar.action: Court, Costa, Osumi-Sutherland, Jefferis and colleagues (Frontiers in Physiology, 2023) describe the Virtual Fly Brain web application and API, which integrate cross-registered 3D images, connectomics, transcriptomics, and expression data for larval and adult CNS, with text, click, image, and property queries.
ocar.resolution: Templates cover adult brain, adult VNC, and larval stages; the main adult brain template is described as holding almost 100,000 cross-registered images from 64 datasets (FlyCircuit, FlyLight, CATMAID, neuPrint, and others). Results include linked 2D/3D browsers, ontology-backed term pages (for example WEDPN2), curated split-GAL4s, and bulk downloads with licenses. The authors suggest the pattern could extend to vertebrate atlasing.
ocar.future_work: Coverage and query power will track incoming connectomes and ontologies; vertebrate extension is proposed rather than demonstrated.

summaries.beginner: Fly neuroscience now has wiring maps, gene-expression maps, and thousands of pictures of labeled neurons, but they live in different websites. Virtual Fly Brain puts those layers on shared 3D templates so you can click a cell, see what it connects to, and find genetic tools that target it.
summaries.intermediate: Court et al. (Frontiers in Physiology, 2023) present Virtual Fly Brain (virtualflybrain.org) as a FAIR atlas of the Drosophila nervous system. Users search by name, location, connectivity, image, or properties (for example dopaminergic neuron, or synaptic input in the antennal lobe). The adult brain template is described as integrating almost 100,000 images from 64 datasets, including EM and light-level neurons, clones, and expression patterns from FlyCircuit, FlyLight, CATMAID, and neuPrint. Term pages combine synonyms, classification, literature descriptions, and reagents; images can be downloaded with licensing metadata. The same idea is sketched for vertebrate atlases.
summaries.advanced: VFB is an integration and ontology layer, not a new connectome. Counts such as almost 100,000 images on the adult template will drift as imports continue; they describe the resource at publication time. Query quality depends on registration and on community curation of cell-type names. Search-by-image and connectivity queries inherit errors in source reconstructions. Vertebrate extensibility is a design claim, not a shipped mouse atlas.

plain_language_summary: Fly neuroscience now has wiring maps, gene-expression maps, and thousands of pictures of labeled neurons, but they live in different websites. Virtual Fly Brain puts those layers on shared 3D templates so you can click a cell, see what it connects to, and find genetic tools that target it.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes can be treated as directed graphs with colored edges (for example excitatory versus inhibitory), so enumerating all small subgraphs could reveal motifs nobody hypothesized.
ocar.challenge: Exact subgraph enumeration is expensive on dense wiring diagrams, and most tools ignore edge types that change a motif’s function.
ocar.action: Matejek, Wei, Chen, Tsourakakis, Mitzenmacher, and Pfister (Scientific Reports, 2022) present a parallel general-purpose enumerator, a divide-and-conquer community strategy for per-region counts, and edge-type differentiation, run on eleven connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They publish overviews of 26 trillion enumerated subgraphs that required approximately 9.25 years of computation time. Ten connectomes come from two C. elegans longitudinal studies; they also discuss a fruit-fly graph with over 21,000 neurons and 800,000 moderate and strong synaptic connections. Known frequent motifs such as feed-forward loops and reciprocal connections are noted as cross-species regularities they hope to complement with new discoveries from the public counts.
ocar.future_work: Larger brains will need further algorithmic ideas, including dividing by functional region; the authors offer the motif tables for longitudinal and comparative follow-up.

summaries.beginner: Once a brain map is a network of cells and connections, you can count every small repeating pattern, including whether a connection is a ‘go’ or ‘stop’ type. This team did that counting at huge scale on eleven wiring diagrams and posted the catalogs so others can look for unexpected motifs.
summaries.intermediate: Matejek et al. (Scientific Reports, 2022) develop parallel subgraph enumeration for connectomes, including edge colors and a community-based divide-and-conquer mode for regional counts. They run the method on eleven connectomes and release summaries of 26 trillion subgraphs, using about 9.25 years of compute. Ten datasets are C. elegans longitudinal reconstructions; discussion also cites a fruit-fly connectome with over 21,000 neurons and 800,000 moderate/strong connections. The scientific goal is un-hypothesized motif discovery rather than only testing classic feed-forward and reciprocal motifs. Runtime relates non-linearly to neighborhood size, which they try to control by reducing neighborhood-size variance.
summaries.advanced: Enumeration counts graph isomorphism classes; biological function is not assigned. Edge-color meaning depends on how excitatory/inhibitory labels were obtained in each source connectome. 26 trillion subgraphs and 9.25 compute-years are aggregate engineering figures, not a claim of 26 trillion distinct biological circuits. Community splits can miss motifs that cross region boundaries. Exact enumeration remains sensitive to proofreading state and synapse-threshold choices in the input graphs.

plain_language_summary: Once a brain map is a network of cells and connections, you can count every small repeating pattern, including whether a connection is a ‘go’ or ‘stop’ type. This team did that counting at huge scale on eleven wiring diagrams and posted the catalogs so others can look for unexpected motifs.

ocar.opportunity: A synapse-resolution adult fly reconstruction with tens of thousands of neurons lets community detection ask how modules nest from thousands of cells down to tens, without choosing a single scale in advance.
ocar.challenge: Prior descriptions of brain organization traded coarse large-scale maps against fine small-scale wiring, and analyzing >20,000 neurons and 10 million synapses needs scalable, interpretable clustering.
ocar.action: Kunin, Guo, Bassler, Pitkow, and Josić (bioRxiv, 2022) maximize a generalized modularity density to resolve Hemibrain communities across scales, recovering sensory pathways, layered fan-shaped-body structure, and a modular superior neuropil with distinct up- and downstream clusters.
ocar.resolution: They find hierarchical organization in which large communities contain smaller ones, automatically recover known anatomy, and report finer fan-shaped-body connectivity to upstream and downstream areas plus a novel superior-neuropil pathway layout. Adding node labels reveals cell-type-specific wiring; an example at χ = 0.75 shows spatial tiling of MC61 cells converging on TuBu cells. They validate the approach on the larval mushroom body against prior structure.
ocar.future_work: They treat other community-detection methods as complementary, warn that reconstruction errors and volume incompleteness (for example a cluster at the cut edge of the volume) can bias clusters, and offer the partitions as hypotheses for physiology and genetics.

summaries.beginner: A fly hemibrain wiring map is so big that it is hard to see the natural groups of cells. This team uses a clustering method that looks at many zoom levels and finds nested communities, including known sensory paths and a layered navigation center, plus some new groupings.
summaries.intermediate: Kunin et al. (bioRxiv, 2022) apply generalized-modularity-density community detection to the adult female Drosophila Hemibrain (>20,000 neurons, 10 million synapses). Communities are resolved from thousands of neurons down to tens, revealing hierarchy. The method recovers sensory pathways and the layered fan-shaped body, and it proposes modular pathways in the superior neuropil. With cell-type labels, clusters can match known types (for example MC61 mosaics onto TuBu). Comparison with spectral embedding is that modularity tends to yield mixed-type anatomical communities rather than single-type clusters. A larval mushroom-body check is used as validation against prior work.
summaries.advanced: The PDF is a bioRxiv preprint (catalogued under Journal of Neuroscience). Modularity maximization finds densely connected groups relative to a random null; other algorithms would highlight different structure. Incompleteness of Hemibrain (truncated neurons at volume edges) can create spurious clusters; the authors discuss keeping an edge cluster because it marks a lobula-plate fragment. Small communities of a few nodes could be noise unless they show reliable cell-type composition. Functional predictions are unsupervised and need physiology.

plain_language_summary: A fly hemibrain wiring map is so big that it is hard to see the natural groups of cells. This team uses a clustering method that looks at many zoom levels and finds nested communities, including known sensory paths and a layered navigation center, plus some new groupings.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale EM images and dense segmentations need meshes, skeletons, and multi-resolution image pyramids for visualization and analysis, produced economically on cloud or cluster hardware.
ocar.challenge: Open tools for large-scale meshing, skeletonization, and data management had been missing even as Drosophila whole-brain/hemibrain, MICrONS cubic-millimeter, and human cortical volumes appeared.
ocar.action: Silversmith, Zlateski, Bae, Tartavull, Kemnitz, Wu, and Seung (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2022) present Igneous, a Python distributed-computing framework for meshing, skeletonization, image-hierarchy creation, and data management, and they characterize performance and storage.
ocar.resolution: Igneous is described as horizontally scalable on cloud or cluster, using compression-aware workflows tied to the broader CloudVolume/Neuroglancer ecosystem. The paper sketches the computing model, usage, and quality checks (mesh volume versus voxel volume, centroid comparisons, skeleton property checks).
ocar.future_work: The resource is infrastructure for existing and future petascale volumes; the authors also tabulate how Igneous sits among visualization and proofreading tools rather than replacing proofreading itself.

summaries.beginner: Once a computer has colored in every cell in a giant brain picture, you still need 3D surfaces and stick-figure skeletons to look at and analyze those cells. Igneous is open software that builds those objects in bulk on a computing cluster or in the cloud.
summaries.intermediate: Silversmith et al. (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2022) introduce Igneous as a Python framework for distributed meshing, neuron skeletonization, hierarchical downsampling, and data management of dense EM segmentations. They motivate the tool with whole-brain and hemibrain fly volumes, MICrONS mouse visual cortex, and a petascale human cortical fragment. The system is designed to scale horizontally and to be economical, with attention to compression and cloud object storage. The paper reports how to run jobs and how they assess mesh and skeleton quality relative to voxel labels. Keywords list meshing, skeletonization, connectomics, cloud computing, and compression.
summaries.advanced: Igneous consumes segmentations; it does not itself proofread merge/split errors. Quality metrics in the supplement (mesh-to-voxel volume ratios, centroid offsets, thinning comparisons, ‘beehive’ skeleton examples) are engineering checks, not biological accuracy of the underlying segmentation. Catalog metadata list Kubota and Raghavan among authors because they appear as editor/reviewer on the PDF; the paper authors are Silversmith et al. Horizontal scaling claims should be read as demonstrated in the authors’ deployments, not as a guarantee for every cluster configuration.

plain_language_summary: Once a computer has colored in every cell in a giant brain picture, you still need 3D surfaces and stick-figure skeletons to look at and analyze those cells. Igneous is open software that builds those objects in bulk on a computing cluster or in the cloud.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain cellular-resolution imaging in C. elegans, Drosophila, and larval zebrafish now records sensory, decision, and motor circuits during behavior, opening a physics-facing theory problem of joint brain and behavioral dynamics.
ocar.challenge: Most neuroscience still studies small circuits, yet natural behaviors (navigation, mating, hunting) only fully exist in freely moving animals whose sensations depend on their own actions.
ocar.action: Lin, Witvliet, Hernandez-Nunez, Linderman, Samuel, and Venkatachalam (Nature Reviews Physics, 2022) review experimental whole-brain methods and theoretical strategies, emphasizing that brain activity is organized by sensory drive, internal state, and both synaptic and non-synaptic connectivity, including the connectome.
ocar.resolution: They argue for pairing top-down computational theories with bottom-up structure in high-dimensional activity, using small genetically tractable animals as comprehensive models. The conclusion stresses that worms, flies, and fish diverged over 400 million years ago, so shared dynamical principles would be broadly informative, while larger animals still require more compartmentalized recordings.
ocar.future_work: Continued sensor, optics, and modeling advances are needed to close remaining gaps between ethology and high-dimensional neural data.

summaries.beginner: To understand real behavior, it helps to watch almost every brain cell while an animal moves, not just a few cells in a dish. This review explains how that is now possible in worms, flies, and young fish, and why theories must include both the wiring diagram and the animal’s changing actions.
summaries.intermediate: Lin et al. (Nature Reviews Physics, 2022) survey whole-brain cellular-resolution imaging during behavior in C. elegans, Drosophila, and larval zebrafish. They argue that natural behaviors make brain activity and movement mutually contingent, so recordings in freely moving animals capture signaling pathways that restrained preparations miss. Organizing mechanisms include sensory input, internal state, synaptic connectomes, molecular synaptic properties, and non-synaptic state organization. Modeling is presented as multiscale, with both theory-first and data-first strategies. The review is aimed at physicists entering systems neuroscience as well as neuroscientists needing theoretical tools.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. It does not report a new connectome or a new imaging dataset. ‘Whole-brain’ in fly and fish is still constrained by optical access and neuron count relative to the worm. Connectomes are one organizing principle among others; the authors warn against ignoring neuromodulation and extrasynaptic signaling. Analogies between small-animal behaviors and those of larger animals are heuristic.

plain_language_summary: To understand real behavior, it helps to watch almost every brain cell while an animal moves, not just a few cells in a dish. This review explains how that is now possible in worms, flies, and young fish, and why theories must include both the wiring diagram and the animal’s changing actions.

ocar.opportunity: Neurons, mitochondria, and synapses in EM volumes carry overlapping biological constraints, so reconstructing them independently throws away information that could regularize agglomeration.
ocar.challenge: Single-cue hierarchical agglomeration is brittle when membranes, z-resolution, or organelle segmentations err.
ocar.action: Hong, Liu, Shen, Chen, Xie, Han and colleagues (BMC Bioinformatics, 2022) define connectivity consensus between cellular and subcellular structures and pose a joint graph-partitioning model that reconstructs ultrastructure and neurons in one optimization, tested on public datasets including SNEMI.
ocar.resolution: They report that the joint model outperforms existing hierarchical agglomeration algorithms on several public datasets. Confidence parameters weight structures by initial segmentation quality; 2D instance contours on ultrastructure reduce under-segmentation risk. Mitochondria supply link cues and synapses supply not-link cues that they say could extend to somata and axon–dendrite relations.
ocar.future_work: They plan tests on other organelles and want to add long-range (lifted multicut) relationships between non-adjacent nodes.

summaries.beginner: Computers usually color neurons and their inner parts as separate jobs, even though a mitochondrion should not jump between two cells. This paper ties those jobs together so membrane and organelle clues vote in one step, which they say makes the neuron maps more accurate.
summaries.intermediate: Hong et al. (BMC Bioinformatics, 2022) introduce a joint optimization for 3D agglomeration in EM that enforces connectivity consensus between neurons and ultrastructure. A single graph-partitioning objective updates neuronal membrane grouping and organelle grouping together, rather than piping independent reconstructions. On public datasets the method outperforms hierarchical agglomeration baselines; SNEMI results are shown with VI and ARE versus a confidence factor. Superpixel approaches are argued to be more robust to local membrane defects than voxel methods, while under-segmented mitochondria can still induce neuronal merge errors if two cells share an organelle fragment.
summaries.advanced: Gains are versus hierarchical agglomeration on public EM benchmarks, not a demonstration on petascale production connectomes. Performance still depends on imaging quality, anisotropy, and watershed over-segmentation settings; the authors say under-segmentation is generally avoided by tuning, not solved by agglomeration. Confidence weights are additional hyperparameters. Extension to somata or axon–dendrite not-link cues is proposed, not shown. Biological plausibility is a modeling prior, not independent biological validation.
