ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes and confocal driver-line libraries describe overlapping Drosophila neurons in different modalities, so a fast morphology search could link a reconstructed cell to reagents that target it.
ocar.challenge: Building a split-GAL4 pair that isolates one EM neuron still requires finding lines whose expression overlap is unique to that cell, which is hard to do by eye across large image sets.
ocar.action: Clements, Goina, Hubbard, Kawase, Olbris, Otsuna, Svirskas, and Rokicki (BMC Bioinformatics, 2024) present NeuronBridge, a web application with a serverless cloud architecture and massively parallel image search (color-depth MIP and PPPM), plus open APIs and data.
ocar.resolution: The service is described as filling a workflow gap between Hemibrain and MANC connectomes and FlyLight driver characterization, used by hundreds of researchers, with code, APIs, and processed datasets available at neuronbridge.janelia.org under a BSD-3-Clause license. Versioned S3 JSON endpoints expose matches by body ID, driver line, and search method.
ocar.future_work: Modular code and open data are offered for reuse as new EM and LM sets appear; the paper is a resource description rather than a new matching algorithm paper alone.

summaries.beginner: If you find an interesting cell in a fly electron-microscope map, you still need a genetic tool that lights up that cell. NeuronBridge is a website that searches light-microscope pictures of fly driver lines to find shapes that look like your cell.
summaries.intermediate: Clements et al. (BMC Bioinformatics, 2024; Janelia) describe NeuronBridge, a GUI and serverless backend for morphological matching between EM reconstructions and confocal driver-line imagery. Color-depth MIP (CDM) search and PPPM search precompute matches that the website and an S3 REST API return by EM body ID or driver line. The authors emphasize Hemibrain, MANC, and FlyLight as the motivating large datasets. Software is Java, JavaScript, and Python, BSD-3-Clause, with versioned JSON schemas so clients can pin API versions. They report use by hundreds of neuroscience researchers worldwide.
summaries.advanced: Matches are putative morphological similarities, not guaranteed genetic intersections sufficient for a clean split-GAL4. Search quality depends on registration into common templates and on which datasets have been ingested. ‘Hundreds of users’ is a usage claim, not a benchmark of ranking precision. Catalog metadata list a 2022 bioRxiv identity; the PDF is the 2024 BMC Bioinformatics software article.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic-resolution graphs now exceed laptop RAM, and comparative queries across regions and species need reusable algorithms rather than one database per dataset.
ocar.challenge: neuPrint and FlyBrainLab work well for specific volumes, but general larger-than-RAM analysis and low-maintenance comparative search remain gaps.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Johnson, Wester, and Gray-Roncal (bioRxiv, 2022) describe a tool suite: MossDB for immutable annotations, Grand for larger-than-RAM graph prototyping with NetworkX/Cypher/DotMotif dialects, GrandIso-Cloud for out-of-core motif queries, and Motif Studio for public cross-connectome queries, interfacing with neuPrint, Neo4j, Pandas, and NetworkX.
ocar.resolution: They emphasize write-once/run-anywhere algorithm design and include a table of connectome sizes from Bock through H01 (Hemibrain v1.2: 21,692 sources; MICrONS Minnie65: 106,126 sources; H01: 1,268,187 sources), noting that density tends to fall as graphs grow. Operational cost and expertise barriers are treated as first-class design constraints.
ocar.future_work: The preprint offers recommendations for community tooling rather than a single production hosted connectome; uptake depends on maintaining the backends as datasets grow.

summaries.beginner: Modern wiring diagrams are too big to hold in a normal computer’s memory, and they live in different databases. This team shares a set of open tools so scientists can search for repeated connection patterns across those huge graphs without building a new system each time.
summaries.intermediate: Matelsky et al. (bioRxiv, 2022) present scalable graph-analysis tools for connectomics: MossDB, Grand, GrandIso-Cloud, and Motif Studio, plus visualization and query services that wrap existing stores. Grand translates NetworkX-style operations, Cypher, and DotMotif into backends (SQLite, Pandas, graph toolkits) so prototypes can move from laptops to cloud graphs. They contrast persistent graph databases (fast but costly to keep up) with on-disk edgelists (cheaper but expert-heavy). A size table lists unique sources/targets and densities for datasets from White/Kasthuri/Helmstaedter/Takemura through Hemibrain, MICrONS Minnie65, and H01. The goal is algorithm and dataset reuse for comparative connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint software framework, not a new biological finding. Table densities mix proofread and unproofread graphs and omit synaptic isolates, as the caption states. Interoperability claims depend on community maintenance of adapters as neuPrint schemas evolve. Larger-than-RAM performance is architectural; the selected text does not quote a single latency SLA. Motif Studio’s public query power is only as complete as ingested graphs.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM is producing ever larger annotated tissues, so labs need an open, cost-aware pipeline that turns dense segmentations into queryable synaptic connectomes on HPC or rented clouds.
ocar.challenge: Prior tools covered pieces of reconstruction, proofreading, and organelle detection, but an efficient annotated-connectome toolkit that neuroscientists can run on existing clusters was lacking.
ocar.action: Schubert, Dorkenwald, Januszewski, Kornfeld and colleagues (Nature Methods, 2022) introduce SyConn2, which starts from dense neuron reconstructions and semantic voxel classes (cells, extracellular space, synapses, organelles), detects contact sites, scores synapses with ultrastructural features, and supports point-cloud morphology, cell-type classification, and a web client, tested on datasets with more than 10 million synapses including zebra finch tissue.
ocar.resolution: Cloud cost is estimated at about US$2,000 per teravoxel of 8-bit raw VEM at 10 × 10 × 25 nm³ (about US$800 per million µm³) on Google Cloud for a zebra finch dataset. Analyses include synapse-to-mitochondrion distance CDFs in pallidal-like versus striatal-like neurons and supervised putative cell-type classification. The package is a major upgrade of earlier SyConn software.
ocar.future_work: SyConn2 assumes existing dense neuron reconstructions; scaling queries and classification as volumes grow remains an operations problem the authors address with chunked CPU/GPU workers (SLURM).

summaries.beginner: After cells in an electron-microscope volume are colored in, someone still has to find the synapses and ask which cell types they belong to. SyConn2 is open software that does that bookkeeping at large scale, including on songbird brain data with more than ten million synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Schubert et al. (Nature Methods, 2022) present SyConn2, an open-source toolkit for dense synaptic connectivity inference from volume EM that runs on HPC or cloud clusters. Processing uses semantic voxel maps, contact-site detection, and additional ultrastructural features around candidate clefts rather than overlap alone. Morphology is analyzed with point clouds instead of only dense volumes. The authors report tests on connectomes with more than 10 million synapses, a web visualizer, and a Google Cloud cost of about US$2,000 per teravoxel at 10 × 10 × 25 nm³ on zebra finch data. Example analyses include cell-type classification and mitochondria–synapse distances in songbird basal ganglia-like circuitry.
summaries.advanced: SyConn2 requires a dense neuron segmentation as input; it does not replace proofreading of that segmentation. Cost figures are approximate cloud estimates for a specific voxel size and dataset. Putative cell types (LTS, FS, TAN, NGF, STN-like, GP-like, MSN) are classifier outputs. Feature-based synapse decisions can still err where ultrastructure is ambiguous. The brief communication format limits methodological detail relative to a full pipeline paper; see the supplement for comparisons to SyConn1.

SyConn2 is open software that does that bookkeeping at large scale, including on songbird brain data with more than ten million synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Expansion microscopy can physically magnify tissue so diffraction-limited light microscopes resolve synapses, potentially yielding optical connectomes with molecular labels that EM struggles to provide.
ocar.challenge: Synapses are small and dense; EM connectomes are limited to small samples and heavy tracing, while ordinary light microscopy cannot separate packed contacts.
ocar.action: Sneve and Piatkevich (Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience, 2022) review ExM-compatible fluorescent probes and labeling strategies for postsynaptic scaffolds and receptors, presynaptic terminals and vesicles, and snapshots of synaptic activity in mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans, including delivery vectors and practical limits.
ocar.resolution: They argue ExM plus multicolor neuronal and synaptic labeling could enable more automated circuit tracing than EM. The perspective stresses that one connectome cannot represent a species, sex, stage, or mutant, and that zebrafish and rodents still lack anything like a complete connectome because EM remains slow and costly.
ocar.future_work: Emerging probes and ExM variants are discussed as the path to multiple optical connectomes per species; the review does not itself reconstruct a circuit.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can see every synapse but not easily the molecules in them, and they are slow. This review surveys dyes and genetic tags that still work after brain tissue is swollen in a gel, so ordinary light microscopes might map connections with molecular color.
summaries.intermediate: Sneve and Piatkevich (Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience, 2022) review expansion microscopy as a route to synapse-resolution optical connectomics. They catalog genetically encoded and other fluorescent probes, compatible with current ExM protocols, for labeling postsynaptic scaffolds/receptors, presynaptic terminals/vesicles, and activity snapshots in mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans, plus vectors and experimental caveats. EM is acknowledged as the nanoscale gold standard but is limited by sample size and tracing burden. The outlook is that ExM could let many labs generate connectomes, including many individuals, if labeling and automated tracing mature.
summaries.advanced: This is a review and perspective, not a demonstrated whole-brain optical connectome. Probe performance after expansion (brightness, linkage error, completeness) is species- and protocol-dependent; the authors discuss limitations rather than a single recommended stack. ‘Fully automated’ tracing is aspirational. Claims about EM sample-size limits reflect the literature at writing time (worm, tadpole, fly, small mammalian pieces).

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM produces tens of terabytes per day, so 2D stitching and 3D alignment must keep up with the microscope if reconstruction is not to stall.
ocar.challenge: Assembling up to on the order of 10^8 tiles into a high-fidelity volume, including a cubic millimeter of cortex, requires automation, distributed compute, and quality control without rendering every intermediate image.
ocar.action: Mahalingam, Torres, Collman, da Costa and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2021) present ASAP (Assembly Stitching and Alignment Pipeline), built on Janelia Render services from the adult Drosophila brain assembly, operating on image metadata and transforms in a database, with BlueSky-triggered workflows, automated QC, 3D alignment (EM aligner), and final render-to-disk, plus multi-channel support for fluorescence and array tomography.
ocar.resolution: They report continuous processing of mouse visual cortex and human samples, including one cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex, at speeds exceeding imaging. A cubic millimeter at 4 × 4 × 40 nm³ is described as more than a petabyte and more than 100 million tiles. Modularity is intended so new algorithms can be swapped without redesigning the workflow.
ocar.future_work: The pipeline is a production stitching/alignment stack; downstream segmentation and proofreading remain separate. Multi-modal array-tomography support is demonstrated as an extension path.

summaries.beginner: A cubic millimeter of brain imaged at synapse scale is more than a million gigabytes of overlapping snapshots that must be sewn into one volume. This team’s ASAP software stitches and aligns those pictures as fast as the microscope can take them, using a database of positions instead of rewriting every image at each step.
summaries.intermediate: Mahalingam et al. (bioRxiv, 2021; Allen Institute, Janelia, and collaborators) describe ASAP, a modular, distributed stitching and alignment pipeline for large serial-section EM. Built on Render services previously used for adult Drosophila, it stores per-tile transforms in a database so intermediate volumes need not be fully rendered. Components include stitching, automated quality control, 3D section alignment, and export. They deployed it on mouse visual cortex and human EM, including the MICrONS-scale cubic millimeter, claiming throughput above imaging rates of tens of terabytes per day. Multi-channel processing extends to fluorescence and array tomography. Example numbers: >1 PB and >100 million tiles for 1 mm³ at 4 × 4 × 40 nm³.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint infrastructure paper. ‘Speeds that exceed imaging’ is a deployment claim for their production setting, not a portable benchmark. Alignment quality for connectomics still depends on sectioning artifacts and QC thresholds not fully reproduced in the selected extract. ASAP does not segment neurons. Catalog organism tags include fly because Render originated on Drosophila; the flagship deployments described are mouse and human ssEM.
